reference.source: Standard gynaecology textbook and paediatric and adolescent gynaecology guidance
clinicalPearls: An imperforate hymen is a persistent membrane that completely occludes the vaginal opening, and it is the commonest obstructive anomaly of the female genital tract
The classic adolescent presentation is primary amenorrhoea with cyclical lower abdominal or pelvic pain, because menstrual blood cannot escape and accumulates behind the obstruction

Retained blood distends the vagina (haematocolpos) and may extend to the uterus (haematometra), producing a lower abdominal mass and, at times, urinary retention from pressure on the urethra or bladder
Secondary sexual characteristics are normal because ovarian function and the endocrine axis are intact, distinguishing it from causes of primary amenorrhoea due to hormonal failure
On inspection the hymen typically bulges as a tense, bluish membrane, and a rectal or abdominal examination may reveal a pelvic mass of retained blood
It can occasionally present in neonates as a mucocolpos from mucus accumulation driven by maternal oestrogen, seen as a bulging introital membrane
Definitive treatment is surgical incision of the membrane, classically a cruciate incision, to release the retained blood and restore patency, ideally performed electively rather than as an emergency
Aspiration alone should be avoided because it risks introducing infection into a closed collection of blood
reference.pathophysiology: The hymen represents the junction between the sinovaginal bulbs and the urogenital sinus and normally becomes perforate before or around birth. When canalisation fails, a complete membrane persists across the vaginal introitus. Before menarche this is usually silent, but once ovulatory cycles begin, endometrial shedding produces menstrual blood that cannot drain. Blood collects first in the vagina (haematocolpos) and then in the uterus (haematometra), and with time can reflux along the tubes (haematosalpinx). The expanding collection causes cyclical pain and a pelvic mass and may compress the urethra or rectum. Because the ovaries and hormonal axis are unaffected, pubertal development proceeds normally despite the absence of visible menstruation.
additionalDifferentials: Cervical or vaginal agenesis (e.g. Mullerian agenesis)
Obstructed hemivagina in complex Mullerian anomalies
Other causes of primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics
additionalInvestigations: Careful genital inspection to identify a bulging bluish membrane at the introitus
Pelvic (often transabdominal or perineal) ultrasound to demonstrate haematocolpos and haematometra
Magnetic resonance imaging where the level or nature of obstruction is uncertain or a complex anomaly is suspected
Assessment of secondary sexual characteristics and pubertal staging
Renal tract imaging given the association of genital tract anomalies with urinary tract malformations
redFlags: Acute urinary retention or severe pain from a large obstructing collection
Features suggesting a more proximal or complex obstruction rather than a simple imperforate hymen
Signs of infection within a retained blood collection
A pelvic mass of uncertain nature requiring urgent imaging
reference.prognosis: The outlook after timely surgical release is excellent, with restoration of normal menstruation and preservation of fertility; delayed diagnosis can allow complications such as endometriosis from retrograde menstruation or, rarely, infection of the retained blood.
pitfalls: Overlooking imperforate hymen in an adolescent with cyclical pain and primary amenorrhoea by not inspecting the introitus
Confusing it with a transverse vaginal septum, which sits higher and needs different surgical planning
Aspirating the collection rather than performing formal incision, risking infection
Attributing normal pubertal development plus amenorrhoea to hormonal causes and missing an obstructive anomaly
Failing to arrange renal tract imaging for associated urinary anomalies
references: Standard gynaecology reference text on Mullerian and outflow tract anomalies
management: Definitive treatment by surgical incision of the membrane (hymenotomy or hymenectomy) to drain retained blood and restore menstrual outflow
Analgesia for cyclical pain and relief of acute urinary retention with catheterisation when the collection compresses the urethra
Avoidance of simple needle aspiration of the haematocolpos because of the risk of introducing infection
Expectant management of an asymptomatic neonatal mucocolpos, reserving intervention for obstructive symptoms
Surveillance for complications of delayed diagnosis such as endometriosis from retrograde menstruation
Reassurance regarding normal fertility and pubertal development, with gynaecology follow-up
